newsitem.title: USA: No real signs of local economic slowdown -- S.F. Fed.
newsitem.headline: No real signs of local economic slowdown -- S.F. Fed.

text.p: The economy in the 12th U.S. district, led by strong activity in California, is running at a fast pace with no signs of a near-term slowdown, said an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.
"As a whole, the 12th district economy looks very good, very strong and there are no real signs of a slowdown," Robert Valletta, economist at the San Francisco Fed, told Reuters.

"At least for the remainder of this year, it looks like the entire district will continue to be strong because acceleration in California is more than offsetting whatever slight slowdown is going on in some of the other states," Valletta added.

The San Francisco Fed serves the nation's 12th economic district, which includes Alaska, Arizona, California, Hawaii, Nevada, Idaho, Utah and Washington, plus Guam, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands.

The 12th district is the largest in the nation, with 1.3 million square miles, or 35 percent of the country's area. The distric ranks second in the system in terms of deposits held by large commercial banks.

Valletta said the 12th district employment rate grew at a firm 3.4 percent in 1996, adding that his personal opinion was that the regional economy would keep the same rate of growth for the rest of the year.

The San Francisco Fed economist said labor markets in the district remained fairly tight. He said, however, that while the phenomenom raises some concern about inflationary pressures, it still was not seen as a bottleneck.
"We are noticing that in some states in particular labor markets are pretty tight," Valletta said.

"It raises concerns about inflationary pressures at the district level and therefore at the national level also, but I don't think there is really clear evidence of bottlenecks at this point," he said.

Speaking specifically about California, the leading and most important state in the district, Valletta said that a long-term slowdown in the technology sector -- the heart of the state's economy -- was unlikely.
"There are no real signs of any slowdown in the ongoing California recovery," the Fed economist said.
"If the technology sector, for some reason, really took a dive that would hurt the California economy because we are so centered in high-tech activities ... But that's unlikely.

"You get ups and down on the technology and computer sector, but on the whole, the trend is upward. People are always finding new applications for computers in both the workplace and in the home," he added.

Valletta said demand for Internet software and communication applications was expected to continue to bolster the California economy, even if some weakness was noted in the computer hardware industry.
"People sometime talk about, in regard to the technology sector, that maybe businesses were reaching the limits of new computer applications and the market is going to slow down.

"To some extent that may be true regarding developing new hardware, but what's really hot these days, what's really propelling growth in the San Francisco Bay area is Internet applications," he added.

The San Francisco Fed economist said labor markets were "pretty much tight" in California. He added, however, that despite recent growth, the state's job market was still lagging the rest of the nation.

"The state is making up for lost time ... but again it just has had so much further to go that in terms of the overall tightness of the labor market, we're still lagging behind much of the rest of the country," Valletta said.
Valletta said unemployment rate in California was 6.5 percent in February, the latest data available, against an average 5.2 percent average jobless rate for the nation.
The San Francisco Fed economist also said public finances in California appeared to be in solid shape, adding that "the state tax coffers are pretty full."
Consumer spending in California was also expected to remain robust through 1997.
"Consumer spending has been pretty strong in the state over the last year or two ... And there is no reason to expect changes in spending behavior," Valletta said.
